summary: Because of unfortunate wording in earlier documents, aggressive use of NSEC and NSEC3 records can deny a name's existence far longer than intended. This document changes the definition of the NSEC and NSEC3 TTL to fix that. It updates RFC 4034, RFC 4035, RFC 5155 and RFC 8198.

eli5.summary: A sign saying nothing lives here should not stay up forever if someone moves in. This document fixes the rules so such no-such-name answers expire at the right time.

questions: what ttl should nsec records have
what is aggressive use of nsec
how long can a resolver cache nsec3 denials
subtitle: Fixes the TTL rules for NSEC and NSEC3 records so that cached 'this name does not exist' proofs expire when the zone operator intended.

tldr.problem: Older DNSSEC RFCs said an NSEC or NSEC3 record should carry the SOA MINIMUM value as its TTL. That can be far longer than the TTL used for negative answers, so a resolver reusing those records aggressively could deny a name for much longer than intended.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC changes the rule to a MUST: the TTL of an NSEC or NSEC3 record is the lesser of the SOA MINIMUM field and the TTL of the SOA itself. It also replaces the TTL advice in RFC 8198.
tldr.outcome: A zone's NSEC and NSEC3 records now expire on the same schedule as its negative answers. The RFC updates RFC 4034, RFC 4035, RFC 5155 and RFC 8198.

facts.label: Required NSEC/NSEC3 TTL
facts.value: Lesser of SOA MINIMUM and SOA TTL

today: RFC 9077 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC. It updates RFC 4034, RFC 4035, RFC 5155 and RFC 8198, so the TTL rules above replace the older wording in those documents.

sections.title: Two Different TTLs for the Same Denial
sections.content:
RFC 2308 says that the TTL of the SOA record returned in a negative answer (NXDOMAIN or NODATA) is the minimum of the SOA MINIMUM field and the TTL of the SOA itself. That value tells a resolver how long it may cache the negative answer.

Meanwhile RFC 4034 said the NSEC record should have the same TTL as the SOA minimum TTL field, and RFC 5155 has equivalent text for NSEC3. The RFC calls this wording unfortunate, because it can give NSEC records a much higher TTL than the correct negative TTL for the zone.
sections.eli5: There were two different timers for the same 'nothing here' message, and one of them could run much longer than the other by mistake.

sections.title: Why Aggressive Use Makes It Matter
sections.content:
Under RFC 8198, validating resolvers may use cached NSEC and NSEC3 records aggressively: they use wildcards and NSEC/NSEC3 records to generate positive and negative responses until the effective TTLs or signatures for those records expire. Before that, RFC 4035 advised resolvers to avoid synthesizing data on their own.

Because of this change in resolver behavior, the correctness of NSEC and NSEC3 TTLs became much more important. That is the reason this RFC raises the requirement level from SHOULD to MUST.

RFC 8198 had tried to fix the problem by telling resolvers to reduce the NSEC TTL to a smaller SOA.MINIMUM. But NSEC records from servers that follow the older RFCs already equal SOA.MINIMUM, so that advice would not change anything.
sections.eli5: Once resolvers started reusing old 'no such name' proofs to answer new questions, it mattered a lot how long those proofs lasted.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC gives a theoretical top-level domain named .example. Its SOA record has a TTL of 900 seconds and a MINIMUM of 86400 seconds.

Negative responses from this zone carry a 900-second TTL, but the NSEC or NSEC3 records inside them carry 86400 seconds. A resolver using those records aggressively would treat them as valid for a day instead of the intended 15 minutes.
sections.eli5: The rule said 15 minutes, but the proof stayed good for a whole day, which is far too long.

sections.title: The New TTL Rules
sections.content:
Sections 3.1 to 3.3 replace the old SHOULD text in RFC 4034, RFC 4035 and RFC 5155. The new text says the TTL of the NSEC (or NSEC3) record that is returned MUST be the lesser of the MINIMUM field of the SOA record and the TTL of the SOA itself, which matches the TTL for negative responses in RFC 2308.

Some signers update the NSEC chain incrementally, so a transient inconsistency between the observed and expected TTL MAY exist.

Section 3.4 completely replaces Section 5.4 of RFC 8198. Validating resolvers are RECOMMENDED to limit the maximum effective TTL of negative responses (NSEC/NSEC3 records) to 3 hours (10800), the maximum default negative cache TTL suggested by RFC 2308. A resolver that supports aggressive use MAY also limit the TTL to the lesser of SOA.MINIMUM and the SOA TTL, and MAY use a previously cached SOA to find these values.
sections.eli5: The new rule is simple: use the shorter of the two timers, and never keep a 'nothing here' proof for more than about three hours.

sections.title: Advice for Zone Operators
sections.content:
If signers and DNS servers cannot be updated right away, operators are encouraged to set the SOA record TTL and the SOA MINIMUM field to the same value. Then the TTL used for aggressive NSEC and NSEC3 use matches the SOA TTL for negative responses.

The RFC warns that some signers use the SOA TTL or MINIMUM as a default for other values, such as the TTL for DNSKEY records, so operators should consult documentation before changing them.

Wildcards are affected too. A resolver treats an expanded wildcard as valid for the wildcard's TTL, capped by the TTLs of the NSEC or NSEC3 proof that shows the expansion is legal. Shortening NSEC TTLs can therefore shorten the lifetime of wildcards.
sections.eli5: If you cannot update your software yet, set both timers to the same number so they agree. Be careful, because that number may also be used for other things.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
An attacker can delay future records from appearing in a cache by seeding the cache with queries that cause NSEC or NSEC3 responses to be cached for aggressive use. This RFC reduces the impact of that attack where the NSEC or NSEC3 TTL is higher than the zone operator intended.

For IANA, a reference to this document was added to the "Resource Record (RR) TYPEs" subregistry for the NSEC and NSEC3 types.
sections.eli5: A trickster could make a 'nothing here' sign stick around so new things cannot show up. Shorter, correct timers make that trick weaker.
